title: Lesson 3: Hallucinations, and How to Catch Them
description: Grounded in Lesson 3 of the AI at Work series — what a hallucination is, its shapes, and habits for catching them.

questions.question: How does Lesson 3 define an AI hallucination, following IBM?
options: A short, obviously broken sentence that is easy to spot by its grammar
Output that sounds plausible but is factually wrong, irrelevant, or entirely fabricated
A rare error that only happens on obscure trivia questions
A software bug that will be patched in the next update
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 uses IBM's definition: output that sounds plausible but is factually wrong, irrelevant, or entirely fabricated. It also debunks the myths that hallucinations only hit obscure trivia or are a fixable bug.

questions.question: Lesson 3 lists several shapes hallucinations take. Which is one of them?
options: Hallucinations can take the form of invented facts and fabricated sources.
Consistently correct answers that are too detailed
Answers that are always shorter than requested
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 lists shapes including invented facts, fabricated sources, wrong specifics, and confident flat wrongness. None of these can be detected by the confidence of the tone.

questions.question: Which habit does Lesson 3 recommend for catching hallucinations?
options: Ask the tool to show its work and express doubt about extra details it adds
Only trust outputs that are written in a confident, assertive tone
Never verify anything because the tool is reliable by design
Generate sources and let the tool create references for you
questions.explanation: Lesson 3's four catching habits include only trusting checkable things, never letting the tool generate sources for you, asking it to show its work and doubt its extras, and doing a second pass on high-stakes output.
